editorNote.lead: This chooser lists ou=policies, and two policies that are deciding right now are not in it. The issuance policy (what this service will issue) and the access policy (who reaches the console, the User Portal, SCIM, the SPIRE Server API) are BUILT IN — called at decision time rather than seeded — so there is no stored document for this editor to open.
editorNote.overridden: One or more of them HAS an override in the repository, so it is in the list above and opens here like any other policy.
editorNote.createBefore: Create one from its template on the
editorNote.label: Two policies are deciding and are not in this list
own.builtInDisabled: the built-in document — the entry {name} exists and is disabled
own.heading: What this service decides its own boundaries with
own.warn1: These two policies are IN FORCE and are not in the table above. That table is ou=policies; these are BUILT IN — the template is called at decision time rather than seeded into the repository — so the editor has never listed them and a reader looking only at the repository would conclude that whatever is root there is what this service enforces. Usually it is not: a seeded example policy decides nothing this service does.
own.warn2: They are built in rather than seeded on purpose. ou=policies is per trust realm, so a policy written once into the default realm leaves every realm created afterwards unable to decide anything at all — and falling back to the default realm's copy would couple two realms, which is the one thing the realm design does not do. Called rather than seeded, every realm has both of them out of the box with nothing to delete.
own.warn3: An override is an ordinary policy. Create one from the same template, named whatever the setting says, and it wins from the next request — it then appears in the table above and in the editor like everything else. Neither is sent to a remote PEP: GET /xacml/pep/policies carries the policies about somebody ELSE's boundary, and these two are about this service's own.
own.warnLabel: Two policies decide here and are not in the repository
noPeps.shared: That does not mean none is running: registering is not what lets a PEP enforce, and one that only ever pulls /xacml/pep/policies works perfectly and never appears here.
noPeps.anywhere: No remote Policy Enforcement Point has registered, in this realm or in any other.
noPeps.elsewhere: No remote Policy Enforcement Point has registered in this realm — but {n, plural, =1 {{n} other realm holds} other {{n} other realms hold}} one:
noPeps.perRealm: . The register is per realm, like the policy repository it serves, so a PEP that registered against /realm/<id> is listed there and nowhere else.
monitor.notReported: not reported — a remote PEP sends what it enforced, and only the process that EVALUATED knows which of the four decisions each was
monitor.notEnforced: nothing was enforced here — this service produced the decision and somebody else's PEP acted on it, in their process
pep.currentTip: This PEP reported holding the repository digest this service has now.
pep.notCurrentTip: The sync token this PEP last reported is not the one the repository has now. It converges on its next poll.
monitor.inProcessTip: Compiled into this process. It is running because this page is.
overview.noRootBefore: No policy is marked as the root, so every decision is NotApplicable. A PDP evaluates one document and reaches the rest through PolicyIdReference, so exactly one policy in the repository is where evaluation starts. Choose one on the
overview.p1: This service is a Policy Decision Point. It is the only protocol family here that answers a question about somebody else’s boundary: every other one authenticates or provisions a person, and this one is handed a subject who was authenticated somewhere else and asked whether they may.
overview.p2: Policies live in ou=policies in the embedded directory. That container is the repository rather than a copy of one, so an ldapmodify there changes what the PDP decides on the next request — and a policy survives a restart whenever persistence.mode is not memory.
overview.p3: The PIP reads attributes off the subject’s own directory entry, so a policy can grant on employeeType without the caller having to assert it. What the REQUEST carries wins over the directory, because a PEP asserting an attribute is describing that request while the directory is describing the world.
overview.p4: xacml.pepBias below is the embedded PEP’s decision and not the PDP’s. Deny-biased and permit-biased agree on every Permit and every Deny and differ on Indeterminate and NotApplicable — which is exactly the case nobody tests, and the reason the setting is here to flip.
overview.label: What this page configures
policies.empty: The repository is empty, so every decision is NotApplicable. Create one from a template below.
template.name: Name for the policy
template.nameHelp: Names the directory entry. The PolicyId inside the document is separate and may be any URI.
policies.p1: ou=policies in the embedded directory is this table. An ldapmodify of xacmlPolicyDocument changes what the PDP decides on the next request, and xacmlEnabled takes a policy out of the decision without deleting it.
policies.p2: Exactly one policy is the root. A PDP evaluates one document and reaches the rest through PolicyIdReference, so the root is where evaluation starts. A repository with none decides nothing; one with two is refused rather than resolved arbitrarily.
policies.p3: A policy that does not type-check is shown in red here and was refused when it was written — XACML is statically typed, so such a policy is wrong for every request rather than for some.
th.name: Name
alfa.heading: Import ALFA
alfa.p1: ALFA is the readable syntax for XACML. Paste one here and it is parsed, converted and STORED AS XACML XML — the repository holds one representation, because two would be two things to keep in step.
alfa.p2: Every attribute must be DECLARED before it is used. That is ALFA's own rule and it is the most useful refusal in the parser: a typo in an attribute name is otherwise a policy that quietly matches nothing, which looks exactly like a policy that is working and denying you. Open any policy in the editor to see the shape.
alfa.label: What this accepts
template.heading: Create from a template
template.p1: A template is the first twenty clicks of the editor already made: a working, valid, evaluable policy in a shape people actually write. The editor takes it from there.
template.p2: blank is the exception and it is here on purpose. It makes no argument and there is nothing in it to read — an empty Policy, or an empty PolicySet, which is the only way to create one of those here without importing ALFA. It denies every request until you put a rule in it, because deny-unless-permit over nothing at all is a Deny. That is the direction a half-built policy should fail in, and it is why building it before making it the root is the right order.
template.p3: RBAC asks what role do you hold; ABAC asks what is true about you, this resource and right now. The first is what most deployments have and the second is what they wanted — having both here, producing documents in the same language, is the clearest way to see what the difference costs in policy.
template.label: What a template is
pep.staleTip: Nothing has been heard from this PEP for longer than xacml.pepStaleAfterS. It may still be enforcing — this service cannot tell.
pep.unauthenticatedNote: Registered with no client certificate, which xacml.pepRequireCertificate allowed. Nothing about this row is proven.
pep.noNotify: none — never nudged, and it converges on its own poll anyway
pep.undischargeable: {n} of those refused for an obligation it could not discharge
peps.p1: A remote Policy Enforcement Point runs in another process, holds its own copy of this engine, pulls the enabled policies from /xacml/pep/policies and decides locally. That is the point of having one: a PEP that asked this service per request would be POST /xacml/pdp with a network hop in front of every access decision.
peps.p2: The pull is the contract. When the repository changes this service also POSTs a few bytes to each PEP that gave a notify URL, saying only that something changed. That is an optimisation over the polling interval and never a replacement for it — a nudge that is refused, blocked or never delivered costs one polling interval and nothing else, which is why the failure is worth showing here and not worth alarming about.
peps.p3: Nothing on this page reaches into another process. “Stop nudging” stops this service dialling that PEP; it does not stop it enforcing, because it already holds the engine and the policy. “Forget” removes the row. Neither takes a running enforcement point out of service, and a console that implied otherwise would be worse than one with no controls at all.
peps.p4: Registering is not a permission. An unregistered PEP can pull and enforce exactly as well; what a row buys is this page and an address for the nudge.
peps.sync: The repository’s sync token is {token}. {current} of {total} registered PEP(s) hold it; {stale} have not been heard from for {after}s.
peps.off: Remote Policy Enforcement Points are turned off (xacml.remotePeps), so the three endpoints under /xacml/pep answer 501 and nothing here is nudged. The register below is untouched and comes back when it is turned on.
peps.notifyOff: The nudge is turned off (xacml.pepNotify), so nothing below is dialled. Every PEP still converges on its own poll — that is what makes this safe to turn off.
peps.cert1: A remote PEP answers its own clients, and the column above is the certificate it answers them with. It is issued by the Remote PEP listeners Issuing CA of this realm — the realm the PEP registered to — so a client that installed this service’s Root CA verifies it, and the chain still says which realm vouched for that front door. It names the PEP’s registered name and the host of its notify URL, plus whatever you add.
peps.cert2: The private key is shown once, on the page that answers the button, and this service keeps no copy. Write the two blocks to the files the container reads (PEP_HTTPS_CERT and PEP_HTTPS_KEY); it picks up a pair written after it started, and reissuing supersedes the certificate it replaces on the issuer’s revocation list.
peps.numbers1: The decision counts are the PEP’s own, reported by it, cumulative in its process. This service did not see one of those decisions — that is what a remote PEP is — so a PEP that restarts makes its counts go down, which is honest rather than broken.
peps.numbers2: The bias column is likewise reported. xacml.pepBias on the settings page governs the embedded PEP at /xacml/protected and nothing here; a control that appeared to set a remote PEP’s bias would silently do nothing.
monitor.hereWhat: Decisions THIS process made, counted as it happened. Since {since}.
monitor.remoteWhat: What registered Policy Enforcement Points in OTHER processes REPORT having done, on their heartbeats, cumulative in their own memory. This service saw none of it — that is what a remote PEP is — and a PEP that restarts makes this half go down.
monitor.combinedWhat: The two rows added up. It is the figure a deployment wants and it is arithmetic over two different kinds of evidence rather than a measurement, which is why it is a row here and not the only number on the page.
monitor.addUp: Allowed + refused + not-enforced = decisions, on every row. The third column is the one that is easy to be surprised by and it is not a failure: it counts the decisions POST /xacml/pdp produced for somebody ELSE’s enforcement point. This service evaluated them and never saw what was done with the answers, so counting them as allowed or refused would be reporting an enforcement it was not present for.
monitor.addUpLabel: Why the three do not add to the total on their own
monitor.p1: This is the only page in this family about traffic. The others are about configuration — what policies exist, what one of them says, what the PDP would decide about a subject you type in. This one answers the question you have when authorization is misbehaving: how many decisions are being made, by which enforcement point, and how many of them are refusals.
monitor.p2: “Decisions” and “allows” are not two views of one tally. XACML has FOUR decisions — Permit, Deny, NotApplicable, Indeterminate — and a PEP has TWO outcomes. What maps between them is the PEP’s bias: a deny-biased PEP refuses a NotApplicable and a permit-biased one allows it, from the same decision on the same request. And an obligation a PEP cannot discharge turns a Permit into a refusal (section 7.2) — the one enforcement outcome that looks like a bug from the client side and is the specification working. So allowed is not permit, and both are drawn.
monitor.p3before: The counters are in memory and start when this process does. They are observations, and this service persists nothing it observes; the durable record of a refusal is the
monitor.p3after: , which holds the reason as well as the count. They are also per trust realm, like ou=policies itself — this page is showing {realm}, and a decision made under another realm was made against another realm’s policies.
monitor.p4: There is no reset button, deliberately: a console that could zero its own monitoring would make every number here a number somebody might have zeroed. A restart is what clears them.
monitor.off: The XACML family is switched off (xacml.enabled), so nothing is being evaluated and every figure below has stopped moving. The embedded PEPs answer ALLOWED without asking the PDP — which is what keeps a service with the family off a smaller service rather than a broken one — and those allows are counted, because they are what happened.
monitor.list1: An embedded PEP is not “registered” and cannot be. It is compiled into this process, so its existence is a fact about the build rather than something it told this service; there are exactly three and they are the catalogue in xacml_monitor.js. A remote PEP registers because it has no other way to be known about — and even that is not a permission: an unregistered PEP can pull /xacml/pep/policies and enforce perfectly, and never appears here. So this list is every enforcement point this service KNOWS ABOUT, which is a smaller claim than every one that exists, and the difference cannot be closed from this end.
monitor.list2: Only the demonstration PEP’s bias is settable. xacml.pepBias governs that one. The issuance and access PEPs are deny-biased by construction — an issuance or an access that was not permitted does not happen — and a remote PEP’s bias is reported by it, because a control here that appeared to set another process’s bias would silently do nothing.
monitor.list3before: The remote rows are a summary.
monitor.list3after: has the sync tokens, the notify URLs, what happened to the last nudge, and the controls.
monitor.listLabel: What this list is, and what it is not
monitor.refusal1before: A refusal here is a policy decision and the reason is in the
monitor.refusal1after: , not in this table: xacml.issuance.refused for the issuance PEP, xacml.access.refused for the access PEP and xacml.enforcement for the demonstration one. This page says how many; that log says who, what and why.
monitor.refusal2before: To make a decision happen on purpose and watch it land here, use
monitor.refusal2after: — but note that the enforcement preview on that page is deliberately not counted. It is a what-if rather than a request anybody guarded, and counting it would make this page’s numbers grow every time somebody looked at it. GET /xacml/protected is the endpoint that really enforces.
monitor.refusal3: Drawing THIS page adds one to the access PEP's count, and that is right rather than a measurement artefact. /admin is one of the five gated surfaces, so reading it is a real request that the access policy really decided — the number would be wrong if it did not move. It is the opposite case from the preview above, and the two are worth telling apart: one is an access that happened, the other is a question somebody typed.
decide.subject: Subject
decide.subjectHelp: A name, a DN or a certificate subject — all three resolve the way they do everywhere else here. The PIP reads this person’s directory entry for any attribute the policy asks for.
decide.resourceHelp: Optional. Becomes resource-id, as an anyURI.
decide.noneApplied: none — nothing in the repository applied
decide.p1: The decision is the PDP’s and the outcome is the PEP’s, and this page shows both because they are not the same answer. A deny-biased PEP refuses an Indeterminate and a permit-biased one allows it; the two agree on every Permit and every Deny. When somebody says a policy “is not working”, it is nearly always because only one of these two was being looked at.
decide.p2: Nothing here asserts an attribute in the request beyond the subject, the action and the resource — so anything else the policy needs comes from the PIP, off that person’s directory entry. That is what makes this a test of the whole path rather than of the engine alone.
decide.label: What you are looking at
editor.emptyBefore: The repository is empty, so there is nothing to edit.
editor.creatingBefore: Creating a policy happens on the
editor.emptyAfter: , in one of three ways: from a template, by importing ALFA, or from the blank template — an empty document with nothing in it, which is the starting point for writing one here rather than editing one somebody else shaped. Come back to this page with it and every element goes in from the menus below.
editor.where1: This editor changes a policy that already exists, and the chooser above is every policy in the repository.
editor.where1after: — there is no New button here, because every control on this page names a stored document and a path inside it, and a policy nobody has written yet has neither.
editor.where2: Three doors on that page: a template (a working policy in a shape people actually write, which is the first twenty clicks of this editor already made), Import ALFA (paste the readable syntax and it is stored as XACML XML), and the blank template — a Policy with no rules or a PolicySet with no policies, for writing one here from nothing. A blank document denies every request until you put something in it, because deny-unless-permit over no rules at all is a Deny; that is the safe direction for a half-built policy to fail in, but it is worth knowing before making one the root.
editor.whereLabel: Where a new policy comes from
editor.liveBefore: This policy is enabled and is the root, so it is what the PDP is deciding with right now. There is no draft state in this editor — the draft IS the stored policy, and every change below takes effect on the next request. That is deliberate: nothing can be lost by closing the browser, and there is no second copy that could disagree with the stored one. To work on it safely, disable it first on the
xpath.one: This document holds an AttributeSelector or an xpathExpression value, and {name} declares no XPathVersion
xpath.many: This document holds an AttributeSelector or an xpathExpression value, and these declare no XPathVersion
xpath.rest: . Section 5.14 says the element MUST be present when a policy uses one. Nothing here will refuse the document — this PDP has one XPath engine and does not choose a dialect by URI, so the decision is the same either way — but a schema validator elsewhere will refuse it, and this is the kind of defect that travels a long way before anybody finds out. The field is on the policy's own row above: http://www.w3.org/TR/1999/REC-xpath-19991116 is what the conformance suite uses.
xpath.label: No XPathVersion, and this document needs one
editor.typeCheck: XACML is statically typed, so these are wrong for every request rather than for some. The policy is stored, but it will not load — the PDP reports Indeterminate and names the first problem.
how.p1: Each row is one element of the policy. The Add dropdown beside it offers exactly what XACML allows at that point and nothing else — a Match may only go inside an alternative, a Condition only on a rule and only one per rule, and the function list on a Match is the two-argument boolean predicates rather than all 275 functions.
how.p2before: Those menus are computed on the server, by the same code that validates the policy, against the real function library — so the editor cannot offer you something that will then be refused. This console runs under script-src 'none' and has no JavaScript anywhere, which is why every control is a form and every choice is a round trip. The cost is real: a five-rule policy built by hand is perhaps forty of them. The templates on the
how.p2after: page are the first twenty already made.
how.p3: Every element you add arrives complete and valid — a new rule has a Target and an Effect, a new Match has a function, a value and an attribute. An editor that produced half-built elements would hold a document that could not be saved, and a document that cannot be saved cannot be evaluated, which is when you most want to look at it.
how.p4: A PolicySet is edited here too, and it holds policies rather than rules. Its children may be a policy written inline, a nested set, or a PolicyIdReference naming a policy stored separately in this repository — which is how a PDP reaches more than one document: the root is evaluated and references are resolved when a decision is made. Its combining algorithm comes from the policy-combining list, which is a different set of URIs from the rule-combining one they are almost spelt the same as.
how.p5: The rest of the syntax is here as well: VariableDefinition (named once, evaluated once per request, visible to its own policy only), AttributeSelector (an XPath over a request category’s content, with the namespace bindings its prefixes need), Function as a value (what a higher-order function such as any-of or map takes as its first argument), the attribute assignments under an obligation, and the optional attributes — Version, Issuer, MustBePresent, ContextSelectorId, XPathVersion and MaxDelegationDepth.
how.p6: Two things are shown and cannot be added. The four combiner-parameter elements are drawn and removable, because a document may arrive carrying them and an element you cannot see is one you cannot delete — but there is no Add button, since section C of the specification says none of the twelve standard combining algorithms takes a parameter, and a control that provably changes no decision would be the first such control on this console. <PolicyIssuer> is not here at all: it belongs to the administrative delegation profile, which this PDP does not implement, so a document carrying one loses it here.
how.label: How this editor works
editor.alfa1: ALFA — the Abbreviated Language For Authorization — is the third rendering of this policy and the one worth reading. Forty lines of XML are eight of ALFA and the eight say the same thing.
editor.alfa2: It is an OASIS Committee Specification Draft rather than a ratified standard: there is no conformance suite for it and no second implementation to disagree with. So the contract here is the one that can actually be kept — anything this emits, it reads back, and the policy decides identically either way — and not that it reads every ALFA document in the world.
form.policyHelp: Version is dot-separated numbers. MaxDelegationDepth is carried and not honoured — this PDP implements no administrative delegation, so the attribute survives a round trip and is read by nothing. XPathVersion belongs in <{defaults}> and the specification asks for it whenever the document holds an AttributeSelector or an xpathExpression.
form.referenceHelp: The id of a policy stored separately in this repository. It is resolved when a decision is made rather than when this document is loaded, so naming one that does not exist yet is allowed — an unresolved reference is reported on the decision. Leave Version empty for no constraint.
form.variableHelp: Every VariableReference naming it is rewritten with it — a rename that left them behind would produce a document that does not load, and the write would be refused. The scope is this policy: a sibling policy in the same set cannot see it.
form.matchType: The datatype follows the function — both sides become {type}.
form.matchHelp: A Match holds an AttributeDesignator or an AttributeSelector and never both. Switching the kind redraws this form with the fields that kind takes. Must be present is the difference between an absent attribute being an empty bag and being Indeterminate — which is the difference between a policy that quietly does not apply and one that fails closed.
form.assignmentHelp: What the PEP is handed alongside the obligation. Category and Issuer are optional and mean "this assignment is about that category" — leave them empty for a plain named value. The value itself is the expression below.
form.xpathHelp: An xpathExpression value is an XPath, and XPathCategory is the request category it runs against. The prefix bindings it uses travel with the document.
form.issuerHelp: An empty Issuer means any issuer, which is not the same as an issuer whose name is the empty string — so clearing the box removes the attribute rather than writing one.
form.selectorHelp: An AttributeSelector runs an XPath over the <Content> of a request category and returns a bag, exactly as a designator does — so most functions still need a one-and-only around it. ContextSelectorId names an attribute holding the node to start from; empty means the whole content.
form.bindingsHelp: . A prefix in the path means nothing without one, and they travel with the document. Type a prefix and a URI to add or change one; a prefix with an empty URI removes it.
form.functionHelp: Named here as a value rather than applied — this is the first argument of a higher-order function such as any-of, all-of or map. Applying it instead is the commonest way to write one of those wrongly.
form.undefinedVariable: Names ${name}, which this policy does not define — so the document will not load. Add a variable definition to the policy, or replace this expression from the Add menu.
form.scopeHelp: Only the variables this policy defines are offered. A VariableReference may not name one belonging to a sibling policy in the same set — section 5.24 — and the document would not load.
